must.text: Safe course: on a TimeoutException (or InterruptException) from commitTransaction(), calls commitTransaction() again on the same producer, possibly several times; retrying is safe and is the only operation allowed after it, and the batch is not processed again.

Says why the PR is wrong: a timeout does not mean the commit did not happen (the EndTxn may already have reached the coordinator); if it completed, the batch's settlements are committed, and processing the batch again from the in-memory start offsets commits them a second time, so the ledger sees duplicate settlements.

If the retries are given up: closes the producer and, after the new producer's initTransactions() has returned (it completes a transaction that had begun completion and aborts one still in progress), rewinds the consumer to the group's committed offsets (consumer.committed(...) then seek, or recreates the consumer), not to the in-memory batch offsets.

Explains the IllegalStateException: after a timed-out commitTransaction() the producer refuses any other transactional operation, abortTransaction() included, until the same commit is retried; so the generic catch must not call abortTransaction() for a commit timeout.

must_not.text: Says that a TimeoutException from commitTransaction() means the transaction was not committed (or was aborted).
must_not.consequence: Believed, it leads to re-processing the batch in a new transaction; whenever the timed-out commit had in fact completed, every settlement of that batch is committed twice and the read_committed ledger books each one twice.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated as fact or used as the basis for re-processing. Does not count when the answer says the outcome is unknown.
must_not.near_miss: A timeout means the outcome is unknown: the commit may already be completing, so retry commitTransaction().

must_not.text: Approves or recommends seeking back to the in-memory batch start offsets and processing the batch again after a commit timeout (with a new producer, or after an abort).
must_not.consequence: When the first commit had completed, the batch is written and committed again: duplicate settlements downstream, exactly what the transactional design was meant to prevent.
must_not.condition: Counts when the rewind target after a commit timeout is the in-memory batch start. Does not count for a rewind to consumer.committed() offsets read after a new producer's initTransactions() has returned, nor for the abort path of an abortable send error.
must_not.near_miss: After closing, a new producer's initTransactions() followed by a seek to the offsets from consumer.committed() is safe.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. The colleague assumes a timed-out commit is a failed commit; Kafka says the opposite is possible. commitTransaction() may have reached the coordinator and be completing, which is why the producer then allows only a retry of the same call. That is why your abortTransaction() threw IllegalStateException. So catch TimeoutException around commitTransaction() alone and call commitTransaction() again in a loop with a limit. If the limit is reached, stop the pod instead of re-processing. The restarted pod's producer runs initTransactions(), which completes or aborts the previous transaction. Its consumer then starts from the committed offsets of the group, so a committed batch is not repeated and an aborted one is. Do not keep in-memory batch offsets for recovery at all.
generic: Transactions in Kafka can fail for many reasons. Handle exceptions carefully, abort transactions on errors and retry, and make sure transactional.id is unique per instance. Consider raising timeouts such as max.block.ms and transaction.timeout.ms so failovers do not cause commit failures.
note: Exception texts are assembled from exact strings: TransactionalRequestResult.await, KafkaProducer.COMMIT_TXN_TIMEOUT_MSG and TransactionManager.handleCachedTransactionRequestResult; the operation name EndTxn(true) comes from the EndTxn handler. b1-07 covered writing the EOS loop and the abort-and-rewind path; this item is about the timed-out commit only. The commit-timeout rule is in the KafkaProducer javadoc (not indexed); design.md holds the rewind-to-committed policy (f8c63106bbb9965f, 3c54eba7e0c0454e).

Says what close(Duration.ZERO) does: it does not wait for pending sends and fails every unsent and unacknowledged record immediately, so the clicks accepted with 202 in the last moments before each pod stops are lost on every rollout.
Corrects the PR's premise: send() only puts the record into the producer's buffer and returns; the record is stored only when its callback (or Future) completes without an exception.

Explains the hang: close() without an argument waits without limit (Long.MAX_VALUE) for all previously sent requests, so the fix for the hang is a bounded timeout, not zero; the kubelet sends SIGTERM and kills the container with KILL when the grace period ends.

must_not.consequence: Believed, the PR is merged: every rollout and every scale-down drops the clicks still in each pod's producer buffer or in flight, although the clients were told 202 Accepted.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or used to approve the PR. Does not count when quoted to refute it.
must_not.near_miss: A record is stored once its send callback reports metadata and no exception (or its Future completes successfully).

must_not.text: Approves or recommends producer.close(Duration.ZERO) (or a shutdown that skips flushing the producer) for the normal pod shutdown.
must_not.consequence: Loses the buffered and in-flight clicks of each stopping pod on every rollout.
must_not.condition: Counts when recommended for the shutdown hook. Does not count when zero is mentioned as what the producer itself uses when close is called from inside a callback, or as a warning.
must_not.near_miss: producer.close(Duration.ofSeconds(20)) after stopping the HTTP listener, inside a 30 s grace period.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. The PR's comment is the bug: a returned send() means 'queued in this JVM', not 'written to Kafka'. With close(Duration.ZERO) the producer gives up on everything queued or in flight and fails it immediately. With linger.ms=50 and steady traffic, that is real data on every pod stop. Keep waiting, but bounded. In the hook, first stop the HTTP server so no new events are accepted. Then call producer.flush() from a separate thread with a 20 s limit and call producer.close(Duration.ofSeconds(5)). Keep the total under terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s), after which Kubernetes sends KILL. Alternatively raise the grace period to 60 s and use close(Duration.ofSeconds(45)).
generic: Graceful shutdown is important on Kubernetes. Handle SIGTERM in the application, configure a preStop hook and a suitable terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and make sure resources such as Kafka producers are closed. Monitor shutdown durations during rollouts.
note: close(Duration) and send() semantics are in the KafkaProducer javadoc (raw_catalogue, not indexed); pod-lifecycle.md is indexed (ad50bee69b25003d). Values (grace period, linger) are invented.

Corrects the PR's claim: CONTINUE means log-and-skip; the record counts as handled, processing goes on and its offset is committed with the following records, so a restart does not process it again; without a DLQ the only trace is the log line (and the record in the input topic until retention, findable only by offset).

Limits what is skipped: the processing handler also skips records that fail because of a bug in the application's own code, so it recommends a custom ProcessingExceptionHandler (or deserialization handler) that resumes only for known bad-data errors and fails for everything else.
Alerts on skipped records with the task metric dropped-records-total / dropped-records-rate (kafka.streams:type=stream-task-metrics) so that skips are seen the next morning.

must_not.text: Says records skipped by the log-and-continue handlers are processed again after a restart or a code fix (because Streams commits only offsets of processed records).
must_not.consequence: On-call relies on the morning restart; the skipped invoices are never added to the totals, nobody replays them, and the invoice totals stay silently wrong.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or endorsed. Does not count when quoted to refute it.
must_not.near_miss: Skipped records are still in the input topic until retention and can be re-read by offset from the log line or replayed from a DLQ.

must_not.consequence: Every malformed or failing record is dropped from the totals without a copy; after retention it is gone, and the error rate is visible only in logs.
must_not.condition: Counts when the recommended configuration skips records without writing them anywhere durable. Does not count for the built-in handlers with errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name set, or for a custom handler that writes DLQ records.

reference:
The PR's premise is wrong. CONTINUE is log-and-skip. The record counts as handled, processing goes on, and its offset is committed together with the records after it. A morning restart will not pick it up, so the invoice would silently be missing from the totals. Today the only trace would be a WARN line, plus the record in the input topic until retention, findable by its offset.

Keep the skip, but never without a copy. Since 4.2 the built-in handlers can write a dead letter record. Set:

props.put(StreamsConfig.DESERIALIZATION_EXCEPTION_HANDLER_CLASS_CONFIG, LogAndContinueExceptionHandler.class);
props.put(StreamsConfig.ERRORS_DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE_TOPIC_NAME_CONFIG, "invoice-totals-dlq");

Each skipped record then goes to invoice-totals-dlq with its raw key and value and the exception, topic, partition and offset in headers. After the fix, replay it into the input.

Do not blanket-skip processing errors. LogAndContinueProcessingExceptionHandler also skips records that fail because of a bug in your own code. Write a ProcessingExceptionHandler that resumes, with DLQ records, only for the known bad-data exceptions and fails for anything else.

Alert on dropped-records-total and dropped-records-rate (stream-task-metrics, info level), so that someone looks at the DLQ the next morning.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Restarting will not reprocess anything: a handler that returns CONTINUE tells Streams to drop the record and carry on, and the committed offsets move past it like past any other record. So the PR trades night pages for silent gaps in invoice totals. Write one custom DeserializationExceptionHandler and one ProcessingExceptionHandler. For the partner's malformed-number case, return Response.resume() with a DLQ ProducerRecord built from context.sourceRawKey() and sourceRawValue(); for any other exception, return Response.fail(). Configure the DLQ topic name for them through your own property. Add an alert on the dropped-records-total task metric, so the morning shift sees there is something to replay.
generic: Exception handlers in Kafka Streams let you control what happens on bad records. Choose between failing and continuing based on your requirements, log errors with enough context, and monitor the application. Consider data validation at the producer side to stop malformed data at the source.
note: Second review: m1 now accepts custom handlers that return DLQ records as well as the built-in handlers with errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name; m2 and n1 cite RecordQueue/StreamTask for the committed offset of a skipped record. The DLQ config exists since 4.2 (upgrade-guide.md:150). Not verified in the pinned sources: whether the DLQ topic must exist beforehand; DLQ records go through the task's record collector like other output (RecordDeserializer.java:122-131, ProcessorNode.java:253-267), and no pinned page says Streams creates it. No point or must-not depends on it; the reference only names the topic. The streams metrics row is in chunk 87a6cc299baa5915.

must.text: Safe course: removes the application-level resend loop, sends each posting once and waits for that send's own outcome (Future.get() without a shorter application timeout, or a callback), leaving retries to the producer, which retries within delivery.timeout.ms; sizes delivery.timeout.ms for the longest failover to be ridden out.

Says the reviewer is right: idempotence removes duplicates only from the producer's own internal retries (same producer id and sequence number); a second send() of the same posting is a new record with a new sequence number and is written again, and a get(10 s) timeout does not cancel the first send, which keeps retrying and usually succeeds as well.

If a send still fails after the producer's own retries, does not resend blindly: stops (or closes the producer) and checks what was last written before sending again, as the producer documentation recommends.

Says idempotence holds only within one producer session: a posting sent again by a new producer (after a restart) is not deduplicated, so duplicates across restarts must be handled another way, for example by a posting id that consumers deduplicate on, or by transactions.

must_not.text: Says that with enable.idempotence=true the broker deduplicates application-level re-sends of the same record, so the retry loop is safe.
must_not.consequence: The loop stays: every get() timeout or failed attempt during a failover writes another copy of a posting, and downstream sums count it twice, as with the three accounts last week.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or used to keep a resend loop. Does not count when quoted to refute it.
must_not.near_miss: Idempotence removes duplicates caused by the producer's own internal retries within one producer session.

must_not.text: Keeps an application-level resend of the same posting after a failed or timed-out send (whatever the timeout or attempt count) without deduplication downstream or transactions.
must_not.consequence: Each resend after a send that did reach the broker adds a duplicate posting; account balances drift by whole postings.
must_not.condition: Counts when the proposed code resends a posting whose first send may have succeeded, with no posting-id dedup on the consumer side or transactional protection. Does not count for resends that downstream deduplicates by a posting id, nor for a resend made only after checking that the first send's record is not in the topic.
must_not.near_miss: Resending is acceptable if every posting carries a unique id and the consumers drop ids they have already applied.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. The author's argument is the common misreading: idempotent delivery protects against duplicates from producer retries, not against your code calling send() a second time. The Kafka documentation explicitly says to avoid application-level re-sends with an idempotent producer. The 10 s timeout makes it worse, because it is much shorter than delivery.timeout.ms (120 s): the original send is still in progress when you send the copy. Replace the loop with a single send() plus a callback that records failure. If the callback reports an error, mark the posting as failed and alert; do not resend automatically. To make postings exactly-once end to end, including after restarts, attach a posting id header and dedup in the consumers, or switch to transactions with a per-instance transactional.id.
generic: Use idempotent producers and acks=all for reliability, and handle send errors with retries and backoff. Monitor the producer's error and retry metrics, and add reconciliation jobs that compare ledger totals with the source of truth.
note: The application re-send and single-session rules are in the KafkaProducer class javadoc (raw_catalogue, not indexed); design.md (952fa5d38ffa9ba6) states the producer id and sequence number mechanism only. Evidence code and counts are invented.

must.text: Safe course: removes the unconditional cleanUp() before start(); KafkaStreams#cleanUp() is meant for a deliberate reset of the application (step 2 of the application reset), not for every start.

Says what cleanUp() on every boot does: it deletes all local state of the application id in state.dir (the PVC) and forces a restore on start; session-counters has no changelog to restore from, so every rollout or crash restart empties it.

Re-enables the changelog of session-counters (removes withLoggingDisabled(), or uses withLoggingEnabled(config) to tune the changelog topic), because without it the store is not fault tolerant and can have no standby replicas: a task that moves to another pod (rebalance, scaling, a replaced PVC) starts with an empty store.
Notes that the changelog of a key-value store is compacted, so it holds roughly the latest value per key; reduce its size by reducing the state or tuning the changelog topic, not by disabling it.

must_not.text: Says cleanUp() only removes lock files or temporary data and keeps the state stores, or that the state on the PVC survives cleanUp().
must_not.consequence: Kept in main(), every pod start wipes session-counters, which has no changelog: the counters restart from zero on every rollout and every crash.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or used to approve the cleanUp() call. Does not count when quoted to refute it.
must_not.near_miss: cleanUp() deletes the application's local state directory; stores with a changelog are then restored from it.

must_not.text: Says a store with the changelog disabled keeps its data across rebalances, task moves or pod rescheduling because it lives on the PVC.
must_not.consequence: Believed, logging stays off: when a task moves to another pod or a PVC is replaced, the store starts empty and the session counters for those devices are silently lost.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or used to approve withLoggingDisabled() for session-counters. Does not count when the answer limits it to the same pod keeping its own state directory.
must_not.near_miss: Without a changelog a store survives only on the instance that keeps its own state directory, and the task cannot be restored anywhere else.

reference:
Don't merge either change; together they lose data on every rollout.

1. Remove streams.cleanUp() before start(). cleanUp() deletes all local state of the application id in state.dir, your PVC, and forces a restore at the next start. It belongs to a deliberate application reset, not to every boot. The lock messages after node failures are a separate matter. Even with changelogs, a wipe on every boot means a full restore on every restart.

2. Re-enable the changelog of session-counters:

StoreBuilder<KeyValueStore<String, Long>> counters = Stores.keyValueStoreBuilder(
        Stores.persistentKeyValueStore("session-counters"), Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long());
        // logging enabled by default; withLoggingEnabled(Map) to tune the changelog topic

Without a changelog the store is not fault tolerant and cannot have standby replicas. Whenever a task moves to another pod (rebalance, scaling, a replaced PVC), it starts empty. Combined with cleanUp() on every boot, the counters would reset to zero on every rollout.

To save broker disk, remember the changelog of a key-value store is compacted. It keeps about the latest value per key, so 1.4 TB reflects the state itself. Shrink that: expire idle sessions, use smaller values, or tune the changelog topic with withLoggingEnabled(config). Don't drop the backup.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. The PVC is not a backup in Kafka Streams' model; the changelog topic is. With withLoggingDisabled(), session-counters exists only in the RocksDB files of whichever pod runs the task; if the task is reassigned, the new owner has nothing to restore from. And cleanUp() deletes exactly those files on every boot, so the counters would not even survive a restart of the same pod. Drop the cleanUp() line; call it only when resetting the application, together with the reset tool. Restore the changelog (the default), and look at why the state is 1.4 TB: compaction already keeps only current values per key, so prune keys of finished sessions.
generic: State management in Kafka Streams needs care. Use persistent volumes for state directories, configure standby replicas for faster failover, and monitor restoration time. Lock errors after crashes are usually transient and resolve on retry.
note: The lock message is the exact format of StateManagerUtil (LockException); the task id and sizes are invented. cleanUp() semantics are in the KafkaStreams javadoc (raw_catalogue); app-reset-tool.md (ba19e763686dbd8f) is the indexed source for its purpose.

must.text: Destructive step with its check: confirms the failure is confined to this one record (always the same partition and offset; the next records decode, for example kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic invoices --partition 7 --offset 48213378 --max-messages 5 shows valid invoices), then catches RecordDeserializationException and calls consumer.seek(e.topicPartition(), e.offset() + 1) to skip exactly that record.

Before seeking, saves the raw record from the exception (e.keyBuffer(), e.valueBuffer(), e.headers(), e.timestamp(), partition and offset) to a quarantine topic or store and waits for that write to succeed, so finance can enter the invoice by hand.

States what the skip costs: after the seek and the next commit, the group never reads offset 48213377 again unless someone seeks back to it explicitly, and the record stays in the topic only until retention (7 days), so the quarantine copy is the durable one.

Explains why retrying does not help: every poll() fails on the same offset because the position does not advance past a record that cannot be deserialized, so the partition stays blocked until the code seeks.

must_not.text: Recommends skipping more than the one confirmed record: seekToEnd, resetting the group to latest, or a handler that seeks past every record that fails to deserialize with no limit and no check of the cause.
must_not.consequence: If the cause is in our deserializer or a producer-side format change rather than one truncated message, every following invoice on the partition (61,000 and more) is skipped and committed: mass invoice loss instead of one manual entry.
must_not.condition: Counts when recommended as the fix. Does not count for seek(e.topicPartition(), e.offset() + 1) after the record has been saved and the failure confirmed as a single record, or for a skip handler that stops (fails) after a small number of consecutive bad records.
must_not.near_miss: seek(e.topicPartition(), e.offset() + 1) for the one confirmed record, after writing its bytes to quarantine.

must_not.text: Says the skipped record will be delivered again later (after a restart, or because auto-commit is off and it was never committed), so it need not be saved before skipping.
must_not.consequence: Believed, the record is skipped without a copy; the next commit moves past it, the group never reads it again and retention deletes it after 7 days: the invoice is lost.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or used to skip without saving. Does not count when the answer says it can be re-read only by an explicit seek while within retention.
must_not.near_miss: A skipped record can be read again only by seeking to its offset explicitly, and only while it is within retention.

must_not.text: Says retrying poll() or restarting the pod will eventually get past the record, and recommends waiting instead of skipping.
must_not.consequence: The partition stays blocked: lag on invoices-7 keeps growing and no invoice of that partition is processed.
must_not.condition: Counts when the answer recommends retrying or restarting as the way past the record. Does not count when retrying is mentioned only as what the current code does.
must_not.near_miss: Retrying cannot help; the consumer has to seek past the record.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Your colleague's rule protects against skipping by accident; here the skip is deliberate and bounded. The exception carries what you need: topicPartition(), offset() and the raw bytes in keyBuffer() and valueBuffer(). Make sure it is one message: run kafka-console-consumer.sh on partition 7 from offset 48213378 with --max-messages 5 and confirm the records parse. In code, catch RecordDeserializationException, store the raw bytes with partition, offset and timestamp in an invoice_quarantine table, and commit that row. Then seek to offset + 1. Count consecutive deserialization failures per partition and stop the consumer above, say, 3, so a format change cannot turn this into a silent mass skip. Note that the bad record stays in the topic only until retention.
generic: Poison messages can block consumers. Validate data at the producer, use schemas with a schema registry, add monitoring for consumer lag per partition, and implement a dead letter queue strategy so that bad messages do not stop processing.
note: The exception message is the exact format of CompletedFetch (it ends with 'If needed, please seek past the record to continue consumption.'), which is why the skip is tempting. The RecordDeserializationException accessors were checked with javap on the pinned kafka-clients 4.3.2 jar; none of this is in the index. The SerializationException cause and the deserializer class are invented.

must.text: Destructive step with its check: after confirming that nothing else in the eta-notifier group needs the skipped positions (only stale pushes would come from them) and that trip-billing is a separate group, moves eta-notifier's position forward for each assigned partition whose next record is older than 2 minutes: seek to offsetsForTimes(now - 2 min) (seekToEnd where it returns null) or seekToEnd, and commits the new position.

Explains why trip-billing is unaffected: positions and committed offsets are kept per consumer group, and seeking or committing in eta-notifier neither removes records from the topic nor moves trip-billing's offsets; the skipped records stay in the topic until retention.

Implements the skip as a staleness check on the record timestamp (skip only when the records reached are older than 2 minutes), or as a one-off that is removed after the incident, not as an unconditional seekToEnd in onPartitionsAssigned, which runs at every rebalance.
Says the skip is a documented use of position control: for time-sensitive processing a consumer that has fallen far behind may skip to the most recent records instead of catching up.

must_not.text: Recommends removing the backlog from the topic itself to skip it (kafka-delete-records, lowering retention, or deleting and recreating the topic).
must_not.consequence: Deleting records, lowering retention or recreating the topic removes the backlog for every group, not only eta-notifier: any positions trip-billing has not read yet, or would need to re-read, are gone for good (recreating the topic also loses all groups' committed offsets), so those trips can be billed wrongly and nothing can be restored.
must_not.condition: Counts when recommended as the way to skip. Does not count when mentioned as what not to do.
must_not.near_miss: Skipping is done in eta-notifier's own consumer (seek and commit); the topic keeps its data for the other groups.

must_not.text: Says that skipping in eta-notifier (seek and commit, or a reset of its group) also moves trip-billing's position, or that both groups have to be reset together.
must_not.consequence: Believed, the engineer resets trip-billing too and it misses 50 minutes of positions: wrong bills.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated or acted on. Does not count when the answer says the groups' offsets are independent.
must_not.near_miss: Committed offsets are kept per consumer group; trip-billing's position is untouched.

must_not.text: Puts an unconditional seekToEnd (or seek to the latest offsets) into onPartitionsAssigned as the permanent fix.
must_not.consequence: Every later rebalance (each deploy, scale-out or pod restart) discards whatever eta-notifier had not yet processed, including fresh positions, so customers miss notifications in normal operation.
must_not.condition: Counts when the seek runs on every assignment without a staleness condition and stays in the code. Does not count for a staleness-guarded seek or a one-off switch removed after the incident.
must_not.near_miss: Seek forward only for partitions whose next record is older than 2 minutes.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Yes, skip; the colleague's rule is for data that keeps its value. Offsets belong to a group, so moving eta-notifier forward changes nothing for trip-billing, and the records stay in the topic. Add a guard in the poll loop: if a record's timestamp is more than 2 minutes old, do not push it. For each partition where the batch is stale, call seekToEnd(partition) once and continue. Commit as usual after the batch, so a restart does not go back into the backlog. Keep the staleness guard permanently and drop any one-off code after the incident; do not put an unconditional seekToEnd in the rebalance listener. Never delete records or shorten retention to get rid of the backlog: trip-billing still needs them.
generic: Consumer lag after an outage can be reduced by scaling consumers up to the number of partitions, increasing max.poll.records and optimising processing. Monitor lag and set alerts so outages are noticed earlier.

Do not merge the PR. The growth comes from clickstream-enriched: its KafkaTopic, created nine days ago, sets retention.ms: -1, so no time limit applies and it keeps everything (about 340 GB on broker 0, all written in nine days).

The PR would not even touch that topic. log.retention.hours is a broker default and applies only to topics without their own setting; clickstream-enriched has retention.ms: -1, which overrides it. What the PR would do is delete, at the next retention check, every closed segment older than 48 hours of every topic on the default. invoices is one of them: billing-weekly-export has not read the last four days (about 400,000 records per partition), so those invoices would be gone and the group's offsets would point at deleted data, to be reset by auto.offset.reset.

Fix it where it is defined:
1. Ask the owners for the retention they need and set it in the KafkaTopic in Git, for example spec.config.retention.ms: 259200000 (three days). Do not use kafka-configs.sh: the Topic Operator reverts changes made outside the KafkaTopic.
2. The closed segments older than three days are removed at the next retention check (log.retention.check.interval.ms, five minutes by default).
3. If you need headroom before that, raise size in the brokers KafkaNodePool (for example 1500Gi); gp3-kafka allows expansion, and the Cluster Operator restarts the pods once the volumes are resized.
4. Watch the volumes fall back to about 55% and keep log.retention.hours at 168.

The disks are filling because clickstream-enriched has no time limit: its KafkaTopic has retention.ms: -1, and it holds about 340 GB per broker. Changing log.retention.hours cannot help, because a topic-level retention.ms takes precedence over the broker default; the PR would only cut the other 45 topics to two days, deleting for instance the invoices that the weekly export (no active members, lag about 400k per partition) still has to read, and that group would then restart from wherever auto.offset.reset sends it. Instead, change clickstream-enriched's KafkaTopic in Git to a bounded retention.ms agreed with its owners (three days is 259200000); the Topic Operator applies it and would undo a kafka-configs.sh change anyway. If the alert cannot wait for the old segments to go, grow the volumes by increasing the persistent-claim size in the node pool; expansion is supported by the storage class and the operator restarts the brokers afterwards.
generic: Disk usage on Kafka brokers is driven by retention. Review the retention settings of your topics and lower them where you can, add disk capacity or brokers, and consider tiered storage for long retention. Monitor disk usage with alerts at 80% and 90% and use kafka-log-dirs to see which topics are large.

Says what lowering would cost: with min.insync.replicas=1 the writes to those four partitions are acknowledged while only their current leader holds them, so if that broker fails before broker 2 or 5 has caught up, acknowledged payment events are lost.

Says acks=1 does not help either: the record is then on the leader only (lost if it fails before replication), and while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas the records are not visible to consumers anyway.

Stops the patching job until the ISR is restored and resumes it only after the check shows no partition below min.insync.replicas (kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-min-isr-partitions empty, or UnderMinIsrPartitionCount 0), so that no further broker goes down meanwhile.

must_not.consequence: Writes to partitions 7, 11, 16 and 22 are acknowledged with a single copy on the current leader; if that broker crashes or loses its disk before brokers 2 and 5 have caught up, acknowledged payment events are gone, or the partition stays offline until that broker returns.

must_not.consequence: Sends are acknowledged by the leader alone; a leader failure before replication loses those payment events, and while the ISR stays below min.insync.replicas the records are not visible to consumers, so the switch also does not get payments to downstream services.
must_not.condition: Counts if recommended as a step, temporary or not. Explaining why acks=1 would be wrong does not count.

reference:
Don't do either change. Partitions 7, 11, 16 and 22 have replicas on both broker 2 and broker 5, so their ISR is down to the leader alone. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 Kafka refuses those writes instead of acknowledging them on one copy: that is the protection you configured, and it lifts by itself as soon as broker 2 or 5 is back in the ISR.

Why not min.insync.replicas=1: acks=all waits only for the current ISR, so every write to those partitions would be acknowledged while only broker 1, 3, 6 or 4 has it. If that broker fails before the others catch up, acknowledged payments are lost. acks=1 is no better: the leader alone has the record, and while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas consumers do not see the records anyway.

What to do:
1. Stop the patching job now so no third broker goes down.
2. Let broker 2 finish its reboot and watch broker 5's startup (journalctl, server.log); after an OOM it may run log recovery first. Fix its heap before the next run.
3. Leave the gateway as it is: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS is retriable, the producer retries until delivery.timeout.ms (120 s), then the gateway answers 503 and checkout retries, so no payment is lost.
4. Check kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-min-isr-partitions (or UnderMinIsrPartitionCount) until it is empty, and only then resume patching, one broker at a time with that check before each.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Leave the topic and the producer alone. Each of the four failing partitions has broker 2 and broker 5 among its replicas, so only the leader is in sync, and min.insync.replicas=2 makes acks=all writes fail rather than be acknowledged with one copy. Lowering it to 1 would make the leader's single copy count as committed (acks=all only waits for the in-sync replicas that exist), and a failure of that broker in the next hour would lose payments that checkout believes were taken. Switching to acks=1 has the same single-copy problem and the records still would not reach consumers until the ISR recovers. The error is retriable and the gateway plus checkout's retry already act as the buffer. Pause the patching run, get broker 2 back and broker 5 through its restart, and continue only when --under-min-isr-partitions shows nothing.
generic: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS means the ISR of the partition is smaller than min.insync.replicas. Check the health of your brokers, look at under-replicated partitions, and bring failed brokers back. Review your producer configuration, retries and timeouts, and make sure your applications handle send failures.

Says a killed broker has not synced its logs, so it runs log recovery when it restarts, which makes each restart and therefore the roll longer, not shorter.

Corrects the premise: the grace period is an upper bound, not a wait; Kubernetes sends TERM and sends KILL only to processes still running when it expires, so a broker that finishes its shutdown in ten seconds is replaced after ten seconds and 0 saves nothing on a clean shutdown.

reference:
Please don't merge this. The premise is wrong and the change makes rolls worse.

The grace period is a limit, not a delay. Kubernetes sends TERM and sends KILL only to processes still running when the period ends, so a broker that completes its shutdown in ten seconds is replaced after ten seconds; 0 saves nothing on a clean shutdown. What 0 does: Strimzi's own reference says a zero value means delete immediately, so the broker is killed with no chance to shut down cleanly.

That costs you twice on every broker of every roll:
- Leadership is not handed over first. With a controlled shutdown the partitions a broker leads move to other replicas and are unavailable for milliseconds; after a kill they wait until the cluster detects the failure and elects new leaders, and producers see errors meanwhile.
- The logs are not synced, so the restarted broker runs log recovery before it serves. Restarts get longer and the 45-minute roll gets longer, not shorter.
- Your acks=1 metrics shipper can lose records that the killed leader had acknowledged but not yet replicated.

Keep the default 30 seconds (Strimzi suggests raising it for large clusters if brokers do not shut down cleanly in time). If the roll is too slow, measure where the time goes per broker (shutdown, startup, catching up) before changing anything; the grace period is not it.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Reject the change. Kubernetes does not wait out terminationGracePeriodSeconds: it signals TERM and escalates to KILL only if the container is still running when the period is over, so a clean broker exit already ends the wait. Setting it to 0 turns every restart into an immediate kill (Strimzi documents zero as 'delete immediately'). A killed broker neither migrates leadership before stopping, so its partitions are leaderless until a new election after failure detection, nor syncs its logs, so it has to run log recovery on start, which lengthens each restart. Records the shipper sent with acks=1 can be lost when their leader dies before replication. Leave the grace period at 30 s, or increase it if shutdowns take longer.
generic: Rolling updates of Kafka brokers take time because each broker is restarted in turn. You can tune the termination grace period and the probes in the Strimzi template, but make sure brokers shut down cleanly. Consider using Cruise Control and monitoring under-replicated partitions during rolls.
note: No any_of. Kubernetes' pod lifecycle page says that forced deletion still gives a small grace period on the node; the rubric relies on Strimzi's own field description ('A zero value indicates delete immediately') and does not claim that SIGTERM is never sent, which is why n2 is worded around the controlled shutdown completing, not around the signal. Second review: the Kubernetes PodSpec description (raw_catalogue swagger.json:10967) states that zero means stop immediately via the kill signal with no opportunity to shut down; added to m1 and n2.

No. It would not unblock refund-auditor, and it would open the cluster.

The error is a missing topic ACL. payments has ACLs (Write for payment-gateway, Read for ledger) but none for User:refund-auditor; the group ACL is already there. allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found works per resource, not per principal: it opens only resources that have no ACLs at all, and resources with ACLs are enforced as usual. payments would stay closed to refund-auditor.    bin/kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 --command-config admin.properties --add --allow-principal User:refund-auditor --operation Read --operation Describe --topic payments

must.text: Main diagnosis: broker 5's replica fetchers fall behind at the evening peak, so its follower replicas lag more than replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s by default) behind and the leaders on the other brokers remove them from the ISR; the URP alert is the symptom, broker 5's follower throughput the cause (its slower volume is the first suspect).

Confirms with read-only checks during 19:00-22:00: broker 5's MaxLag and per-partition ConsumerLag (kafka.server:type=FetcherLagMetrics) against the other brokers, and broker 5's disk write throughput against its volume's limit.

Rejects raising replica.lag.time.max.ms to 300000: the lag time bounds how long a write waits for all in-sync replicas and so how long an acks=all producer waits; with broker 5 kept in the ISR while minutes behind, acks=all writes to the partitions it follows wait for it, longer than the producers' request.timeout.ms (30 s).

Fixes broker 5's follower throughput: gives it disk throughput like the other brokers, or, if its fetcher threads are the limit, raises num.replica.fetchers (cluster-wide dynamic; more I/O parallelism at the cost of CPU and memory).
Verifies afterwards that IsrShrinksPerSec and IsrExpandsPerSec stay at 0 through the evening peak.

must_not.text: Recommends raising replica.lag.time.max.ms to minutes (for example the proposed 300000) to stop the ISR shrinks or the alert.
must_not.consequence: Broker 5 stays in the ISR while it is far behind; at the evening peak every acks=all write to the partitions it follows waits for broker 5 to fetch it (up to the lag time, now five minutes, instead of 30 s): produce latency on those partitions rises to tens of seconds or more, requests pass the producers' request.timeout.ms (30 s) and are retried (duplicates for producers without idempotence), and sends whose wait exceeds delivery.timeout.ms (120 s) fail.
must_not.condition: Counts if recommended as a fix or as a stop-gap, at any value of minutes. Leaving 30 s, or naming the proposal to reject it, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Keep replica.lag.time.max.ms at 30 s; the ISR shrinks are the useful symptom of broker 5 falling behind.

must_not.text: Claims that an acks=all write is acknowledged once min.insync.replicas replicas have it, so a slow follower kept in the ISR does not delay producers.
must_not.consequence: Believing it, the team raises the lag time as harmless; acks=all in fact waits for every replica in the current ISR, so keeping the lagging broker 5 in the ISR stalls those writes into producer timeouts.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or used as the argument that the change does not affect producers.
must_not.near_miss: acks=all waits for every in-sync replica; min.insync.replicas only sets how small the ISR may get before writes are refused.

reference:
The alert is telling the truth: broker 5 cannot keep up at the evening peak. The leaders on brokers 0 to 4 shrink their ISRs (IsrShrinksPerSec > 0 on them, 0 on broker 5, which leads its own partitions fine) because broker 5's followers lag more than replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s) behind; its MaxLag is 412,000 messages against a few hundred elsewhere, and only in the evening. The obvious suspect is its volume: 125 MiB/s against 500 on the others.

Confirm, read-only, between 19:00 and 22:00:
- broker 5's MaxLag and the per-partition ConsumerLag of kafka.server:type=FetcherLagMetrics;
- broker 5's disk write throughput and latency against the gp3-standard limit.

Do not raise replica.lag.time.max.ms. The lag time is what bounds how long a write waits for all in-sync replicas, and acks=all waits for every in-sync replica, not just min.insync.replicas of them. With 300000, broker 5 would stay in the ISR while minutes behind and every acks=all write to the partitions it follows would wait for it, far beyond the producers' 30 s request.timeout.ms: retries, timeouts and failed sends instead of an alert.

Fix the cause: give broker 5 the same disk throughput as the others (for example raise the provisioned throughput of its volume), or, if the fetcher threads turn out to be the limit, raise num.replica.fetchers. Then check that IsrShrinksPerSec and IsrExpandsPerSec stay at 0 through the peak.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Broker 5 is a slow follower: during peak traffic its replica fetching falls far behind (MaxLag around 400k messages), so after 30 s the partition leaders drop it from the ISR and add it back when it catches up, which is the flapping. Check its fetcher lag metrics and its volume (the 125 MiB/s class) during the peak to confirm, then remove the bottleneck: more throughput for its disk, or more replica fetcher threads if the threads are saturated. Raising replica.lag.time.max.ms would hide the symptom by keeping broker 5 in sync on paper; since an acks=all write needs all in-sync replicas, producers would then wait on broker 5 for up to five minutes per write and run into their request timeout. Success is ISR shrink and expand rates of zero in the evening.
generic: Under-replicated partitions mean that some followers are not in sync. Check broker health, network and disk performance, and replication metrics. Tune replica.lag.time.max.ms and the number of replica fetchers if needed, and make sure brokers have enough resources. Alert on sustained, not momentary, under-replication.

must.text: Main recommendation: add a startupProbe with the same check and failureThreshold x periodSeconds longer than the worst-case log recovery (for example periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 180 for 30 minutes); Kubernetes runs no liveness or readiness probe until it has succeeded, so the recovering broker is not killed, and the liveness probe then works as before.

Keeps the readiness probe: a StatefulSet RollingUpdate waits until each updated pod is Running and Ready before it updates the next one, and a container without a readiness probe counts as ready (Success) as soon as it runs, so without it the next broker would be restarted while the previous one is still recovering.

Explains the loop: the liveness probe restarts the container before log recovery has finished, so the broker never completes a clean shutdown and has to start log recovery again on the next start; with 90 seconds allowed, the recovery never gets to finish.

must.text: Optionally raises num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir (2 by default since 4.0) to speed up log recovery after an unclean shutdown, at the cost of more I/O.

must_not.text: Approves removing the readiness probe (or replacing it with a check that passes as soon as the process starts).
must_not.consequence: The broker pods count as Ready as soon as their container runs, so the StatefulSet's rolling update (already the one that applies this PR) moves to the next broker at once, while the previous one is still starting up or recovering and has not rejoined the ISR; partitions with replicas on both brokers are left with one in-sync replica, below min.insync.replicas 2, and reject acks=all writes.

must_not.near_miss: Keep the readiness probe as it is and add a startup probe that covers log recovery.

must_not.text: Claims that a StatefulSet rolling update waits only for the container to be running, so the readiness probe does not affect how the brokers are restarted.
must_not.consequence: Believing it, the team drops the readiness probe; rolls then restart brokers back to back while earlier ones are still recovering, with the rejected writes and offline partitions described in n1.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or used as the argument that removing readiness is harmless.
must_not.near_miss: The StatefulSet controller waits for each updated pod to be Running and Ready before moving to the next one.

Don't remove the probes; add a startup probe.

What is happening: kafka-2 stopped without a clean shutdown, so it has to run log recovery over 1.6 TB before it serves requests. The liveness probe allows 60 s plus three failures and restarts it before the recovery has finished; the broker never gets to a clean shutdown, so the next start must recover again, and so it loops.

The fix is a startupProbe with the same command and failureThreshold x periodSeconds above your worst recovery time, for example:
  startupProbe: (same exec)
    periodSeconds: 10
    failureThreshold: 180   # 30 minutes
While a startup probe is configured, Kubernetes runs no liveness or readiness probe until it succeeds; afterwards the liveness probe still catches a hung broker. The long initialDelaySeconds on liveness can then go.

Keep the readiness probe in particular. Your StatefulSet's RollingUpdate waits for each updated pod to be Running and Ready before it restarts the next one. A container without a readiness probe counts as ready as soon as it runs, so the next chart upgrade would restart brokers back to back while earlier ones are still recovering, and partitions with two replicas on those brokers would refuse acks=all writes or go offline.

Optionally raise num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir (2 by default) to shorten recovery, at the cost of more disk I/O. After merging, watch kafka-2 log the end of recovery and rejoin the ISR before you touch any other broker.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. The probes are right; their timing is not. Recovery after the power loss takes longer than the 90 seconds the liveness probe allows, and every kill starts another unclean restart that needs recovery again. Put a startup probe in front: same exec check, period 10 s, failure threshold large enough for the longest recovery you expect (say 180, which is 30 minutes). Liveness and readiness are suspended until it passes. Removing the readiness probe would be the dangerous part of the PR: an absent readiness probe is treated as success, and the StatefulSet's rolling update only waits for Ready before moving to the next ordinal, so future rolls would take down the next broker while the previous one is still recovering. More recovery threads (num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir) can shorten the recovery itself.
generic: Liveness probes that kill slow-starting containers are a common problem. Increase initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold, make sure the probe command is lightweight, and check the logs of the broker to see why it is slow. Consider using an HTTP or TCP probe instead of an exec probe.
note: No any_of. Raising the liveness initialDelaySeconds would also stop the loop but is not equally good (it delays detection of hangs on every start), so it is neither a must point nor a must-not; the generic answer uses it and still makes no must point. The probe command, the event texts and the recovery size are invented; the event texts follow the forms in the pinned Kubernetes docs (BackOff set to the docs' form at the second review). That the broker does not answer kafka-broker-api-versions during log recovery is assumed, not documented; no point rests on it. Second review: a liveness restart is not a hard kill (probes.md:260), so m3 and the reference no longer say so.

must.text: Main recommendation: keep replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2 and acks=all for order-events; take the disk saving from local.retention.ms (6 hours), which is what tiered storage is for, not from fewer replicas.

Explains why the replicas still matter: only completed (rolled) segments are copied to the remote tier; the active segment, which holds the newest acknowledged records, and segments not yet copied exist only on the brokers' local disks, so their durability rests on replication.

Sizes local disk: about 60 MB/s x 21,600 s, roughly 1.3 TB per copy for 6 hours of local retention, about 3.9 TB at replication factor 3 (around 430 GB per broker over nine) plus the active segments, against 466 TB today; replication factor 2 would save only about another 1.3 TB.

Notes that segment.bytes and segment.ms decide how soon records become eligible for upload, since a segment is copied only after it rolls; a large, slowly rolling active segment keeps more recent data local-only.

must_not.text: Recommends or accepts replication factor 2 with min.insync.replicas 1, or replication factor 1, for order-events because the data is in the remote tier.
must_not.consequence: acks=all writes are then acknowledged with one copy whenever a replica is out of the ISR, and the newest records sit only on local disks until their segment rolls and is uploaded; a broker or disk failure in that window loses acknowledged order events for good, and with one copy the partition is offline until the broker returns.
must_not.condition: Counts if recommended or accepted as part of the design. Keeping replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 does not count, nor does discussing the option in order to reject it.
must_not.near_miss: Keep replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 and set local.retention.ms to 6 hours to cut local disk.

must_not.text: Claims that with tiered storage every acknowledged record is stored in the remote tier (immediately or on write), so the local replicas are only a cache.
must_not.consequence: Believing it, the team lowers replication; the active segment and not-yet-uploaded segments exist only locally, so losing a broker loses the most recent acknowledged orders.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or used as the argument for lowering replication.
must_not.near_miss: Only completed segments are uploaded; the local log, including the active segment, is the only copy of the most recent data.

reference:
Half of the plan holds. Tiered storage with local.retention.ms of 6 hours is the right way to shrink local disk; cutting replication to 2 with min.insync.replicas 1 is not, and it buys almost nothing.

The object store only receives completed segments: a segment is copied after it rolls. The active segment, which holds the newest acknowledged orders, and any rolled segment not yet copied exist only on the brokers. Their durability is exactly what replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 and acks=all gives you: every acknowledged write on at least two brokers. With RF 2 and min ISR 1, a write acknowledged while one replica is out of the ISR has one copy, and losing that broker or disk before upload loses it.

Sizing with the plan's local retention:
- 60 MB/s x 21,600 s, about 1.3 TB per copy of local data;
- at RF 3 about 3.9 TB in total, around 430 GB per broker, plus active segments and headroom;
- against 466 TB today. RF 2 would save only about another 1.3 TB.

Also:
- segment.bytes and segment.ms decide how soon data becomes eligible for upload; keep segments rolling well within the 6 hours.
- Reads of data older than 6 hours (replays, lagging consumers) come from the object store; ask for those read rates.

So: remote.storage.enable=true, local.retention.ms=21600000, retention.ms 30 days, and keep RF 3, min.insync.replicas 2, acks=all.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Adopt tiered storage, drop the replication change. What the remote tier holds is rolled segments; whatever is still in the active segment, or rolled but not yet copied, lives only on broker disks, and the guarantee for those records is the ISR: with RF 3 and min ISR 2 an acknowledged write is on two brokers at least. RF 2 with min ISR 1 lets acks=all succeed on a single broker, so one disk failure can lose orders the producers saw acknowledged. The saving would be small anyway: with six hours kept locally the topic needs about 1.3 TB per copy (60 MB/s for 21,600 s), roughly 3.9 TB across the cluster at RF 3, compared with 466 TB now. Keep segment rolls frequent enough (segment.ms or segment.bytes) that data is uploaded promptly.
generic: Tiered storage moves older data to object storage and reduces local disk needs. Choose a reliable RemoteStorageManager plugin, set local and total retention, and test performance for consumers reading old data. Replication factor and min.insync.replicas are trade-offs between cost and durability that depend on your requirements.
note: No any_of. The pinned docs say the remote tier stores 'the completed log segments' and that the old segment moves after the active one rolls; they do not say how many copies the plugin keeps remotely, so no point sizes the remote tier. 466 TB is 155 TB x 3 from the question's figures; 60 MB/s x 30 days is about 155 TB.

must.text: Main recommendation: reject delete.retention.ms: 0; keep it well above the longest full read from offset 0 (the 55-minute rebuild); the 24-hour default is fine.

Says what it would break: a pod that starts from offset 0 and needs longer than delete.retention.ms to reach the head can miss the tombstone of a key whose older record it has already read, so it keeps the revoked key in its map and accepts it.

Says the part that shrinks what the pods read is min.cleanable.dirty.ratio: at the default 0.5 up to half of the log can be duplicates, and 0.1 trades more frequent cleaning (more cleaner I/O) for less wasted space.

On segment.ms: the active segment is never compacted, so rolling sooner lets recent updates be compacted sooner, but one minute creates a new segment per partition every minute, each costing file descriptors and two memory-map areas; a moderate value (hours rather than one minute) is enough.

must_not.text: Approves delete.retention.ms: 0, or any value shorter than the pods' 40 to 55 minute rebuild.
must_not.consequence: Tombstones are removed soon after cleaning, so a gateway pod that read a revoked key's earlier record during its long rebuild never sees the deletion and keeps accepting the revoked API key until it restarts again.
must_not.condition: Counts if approved or recommended. A value of several hours or the default does not count; quoting the PR to reject it does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Keep delete.retention.ms at the 24-hour default; tune min.cleanable.dirty.ratio to shrink the log.

must_not.text: Claims that a consumer reading a compacted topic from the beginning always ends up with the deletions applied, because compaction removes a deleted key's older records together with, or before, its tombstone.
must_not.consequence: Believing it, the team merges delete.retention.ms: 0; because cleaning runs while the pods read, a pod can read an old record of a key and arrive after its tombstone is gone, so revoked keys stay valid in that pod.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or used as the argument for removing tombstones at once.
must_not.near_miss: A reader that reaches the head within delete.retention.ms sees every tombstone; a slower reader can miss them.

reference:
Not as it stands: drop delete.retention.ms: 0, keep a lower dirty ratio, and use a moderate segment.ms.

delete.retention.ms is not dead weight; it is the window within which a reader starting from offset 0 is guaranteed to see the tombstones. Compaction runs while your pods read. A pod that has already read a key's earlier record and needs longer than delete.retention.ms to reach the head can find the tombstone gone, and it keeps the revoked key in its map and accepts it. Your rebuild takes up to 55 minutes, so the value must stay well above that; the 24-hour default is fine.

min.cleanable.dirty.ratio: 0.1 is the part that shrinks what the pods read. At the default 0.5 up to half the log can be duplicates; 0.1 keeps it much closer to one record per key, at the price of more frequent cleaning and more cleaner I/O.

segment.ms: the active segment is never compacted, so rolling sooner does let recent updates be compacted sooner. But 60000 creates a new segment per partition every minute, and every segment costs file descriptors and two memory-map areas. Hours rather than a minute is enough here.

Suggested config: cleanup.policy compact, delete.retention.ms left at the default, min.cleanable.dirty.ratio 0.1, segment.ms 3600000. Then measure the topic size and the rebuild time again.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Merge the dirty-ratio change, rework segment.ms and remove delete.retention.ms: 0. Tombstones have to outlive the slowest full read: Kafka only promises that a consumer starting at the beginning sees the delete markers if it gets to the head of the log within delete.retention.ms, and cleaning happens concurrently with reads. With 0, a gateway that loaded a key's earlier value early in its 40 to 55 minute load can miss the tombstone and keep treating a revoked key as valid. Keep the default of a day. Lowering min.cleanable.dirty.ratio to 0.1 is what reduces the amount of duplicate data to read, at extra cleaning cost. Since compaction never touches the active segment, a shorter roll interval helps, but one minute multiplies segment files, descriptors and memory maps; an hour is plenty.
generic: Compacted topics keep the latest value per key. To speed up consumers that read the whole topic, tune the log cleaner (dirty ratio, segment size, cleaner threads) and consider caching state locally. Review delete.retention.ms and other compaction settings against your requirements and test changes before production.
note: No any_of. Nearest earlier items: d5-09 (sizing of a compacted state topic) and b2-07 (coding a full-topic cache loader) both carry the delete.retention.ms reading-window fact as one point among others; here the family is a configuration review whose tempting step is removing tombstone retention to shorten loads, and the harm is revoked credentials staying valid. The rebuild times and the topic are invented; the suggested segment.ms value is a judgement, not documented.

must.text: Main step: after confirming that broker 3, the partition's only in-sync replica, and its log are gone for good (the volume is deleted, as support confirmed) and that no other replica is in the ISR, runs an unclean leader election for that partition only, for example kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --election-type unclean --topic shipment-status --partition 14.

States the loss: the elected replica (broker 7 or 8) becomes the source of truth, so the records it lacks that only broker 3 had (written while 7 and 8 were catching up) are lost; waiting cannot bring them back because broker 3's log no longer exists.

Keeps unclean.leader.election.enable false for the cluster; if it is enabled on the topic instead of the one-off election, it takes effect only when the periodic election thread runs (default 5 minutes) and is removed again afterwards.

Afterwards checks the consumer groups of shipment-status: committed offsets of partition 14 beyond the new log end no longer exist and the consumers are reset by auto.offset.reset; the lost window has to be resent from the carriers' side if needed.
Restores three replicas with a reassignment that replaces broker 3 in the replica lists of partition 14 (and of the other partitions broker 3 held) by a live broker.

must_not.text: Recommends enabling unclean.leader.election.enable=true for the whole cluster (the broker default) and leaving it on.
must_not.consequence: From then on any partition of any topic whose in-sync replicas are all down elects an out-of-sync replica automatically, including topics with acks=all and min.insync.replicas 2, so a later broker failure silently loses committed messages instead of waiting for the in-sync replica.
must_not.condition: Counts if recommended cluster-wide, or on the topic without removing it afterwards. The one-off kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type unclean, or a temporary topic override that is removed after the election, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Run the unclean election once for shipment-status-14 and keep unclean.leader.election.enable false everywhere.

must_not.text: Claims that the unclean election loses nothing, for example because broker 7 or 8 will fetch the missing records later or the logs are merged when a broker 3 returns.
must_not.consequence: The team skips the check of the consumer groups and the resend of the lost window; the shipment updates that only broker 3 had are silently missing downstream.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or as the reason no follow-up is needed.
must_not.near_miss: The records that only broker 3 held are lost; the election only restores availability.

must_not.text: Recommends keeping shipment-status-14 offline and waiting for broker 3 to come back, or says the partition will recover by itself.
must_not.consequence: Broker 3's log is deleted, so the only in-sync replica can never return: shipment-status-14 stays without a leader permanently, and every send from the carriers whose keys hash to it keeps failing.
must_not.condition: Counts if given as the recommendation. Saying that waiting would be right if broker 3's disk still existed does not count.
must_not.near_miss: If broker 3's volume still existed, waiting for it would be the right call; it does not.

reference:
Here an unclean election is the right call, for this one partition, after one check.

The runbook rule protects you from electing an out-of-sync replica while the in-sync one could still come back. That is not your case: shipment-status-14's only in-sync replica was broker 3, and its log is gone (volume deleted, support confirmed). Waiting would leave the partition down forever.

1. Check: describe shows Leader: none and Isr: 3 only; brokers 7 and 8 are alive but not in sync. Confirm once more that broker 3's volume is deleted, not just detached.
2. Elect for this partition only:
   bin/kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --election-type unclean --topic shipment-status --partition 14
   Do not enable unclean.leader.election.enable cluster-wide. If you use the topic setting instead, it only acts when the periodic election runs (up to 5 minutes) and must be removed afterwards.
3. Accept and handle the loss: broker 7 or 8 becomes the source of truth, so the records only broker 3 had (about 1.4 to 1.7 GB going by the sizes) are lost. Check the groups with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe: offsets beyond the new log end no longer exist and auto.offset.reset applies. Ask the carriers' side to resend the window if they can.
4. Restore RF 3: reassign partition 14 (and broker 3's other partitions) to replace broker 3 with a live broker.
5. Afterwards, review min.insync.replicas=1 with acks=1 on this topic; that combination is how one broker ended up holding data alone.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Your runbook's rule assumes the last in-sync replica might return. Broker 3 will not: its log has been deleted, so the partition can only come back by accepting a replica that is not in sync. Verify the facts first (no leader, ISR contains only broker 3, volume really deleted), then elect just this partition with kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type unclean --topic shipment-status --partition 14, leaving the cluster's unclean.leader.election.enable at false. Whatever broker 3 had beyond what broker 7 or 8 copied is lost for good, since the new leader's log becomes authoritative; tell the consumers' owners, check committed offsets on partition 14 (offsets past the new end are reset according to auto.offset.reset) and arrange a resend if the carriers keep history. Finally move partition 14's third replica, and broker 3's other replicas, onto a surviving broker by reassignment.
generic: When a partition has no leader, check the state of the brokers that host its replicas and try to bring them back. Unclean leader election can restore availability but may lose data, so it should be a last resort. Review your replication factor and min.insync.replicas to avoid such situations.
note: destructive_right: the destructive step (unclean election) is correct because the only in-sync replica's log no longer exists; the check is in m1. kafka-leader-election.sh's options (--election-type unclean, --topic, --partition) are in the tool's source in the catalogue; the topic config reference in the index names the tool and its unclean option. The sizes are invented; the 1.4 to 1.7 GB is only a hint from them, not a measured loss.

must.text: Main step: lowering is right here; sets ledger-entries' min.insync.replicas to 2 (kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name ledger-entries --add-config min.insync.replicas=2, or --delete-config min.insync.replicas to fall back to the cluster default 2), after checking that every partition has replication factor 3.

Explains why: with min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor, any replica out of the ISR (every broker restart) makes acks=all writes fail; replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 still puts every acknowledged write on at least two replicas and tolerates one broker down.

Makes the change while every partition of ledger-entries has its full ISR (as today), not during a patch run, and notes that with eligible leader replicas enabled (the default on a cluster created on 4.1 or later, as this one) changing a topic's min.insync.replicas clears that topic's ELR state.
Verifies: kafka-configs.sh --describe shows 2 (or only the cluster default), and during the next patch run UnderMinIsrPartitionCount stays 0 and the writer logs no NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS.

must_not.text: Recommends min.insync.replicas=1 for ledger-entries, or acks=1 for the writer, to stop the errors.
must_not.consequence: With min.insync.replicas=1, acks=all writes are acknowledged by whatever replicas are left in the ISR, down to the leader alone: if during a broker restart another replica of a partition falls out of the ISR, writes are acknowledged on one copy and are lost if that broker then fails. With acks=1 every write is acknowledged by the leader alone and is lost if the leader fails before the followers have replicated it.
must_not.condition: Counts if recommended as the change or as a temporary measure for the patch window.
must_not.near_miss: Set min.insync.replicas to 2 and keep acks=all.

must_not.text: Claims that with acks=all a write is always acknowledged by all three assigned replicas of the partition, so min.insync.replicas (1, 2 or 3) only affects availability and not how many copies an acknowledged write has.
must_not.consequence: Believing it, the team sees no durability cost in going below 2 (for example to 1 for the patch runs); acks=all in fact waits only for the current ISR, so with min.insync.replicas=1 a write can be acknowledged by the leader alone and is lost if that broker fails before the other replicas have caught up.
must_not.condition: Counts if stated as a fact or used as the argument that a value below 2 is as durable. Saying that with all three replicas in the ISR an acks=all write waits for all three does not count (that is correct).
must_not.near_miss: acks=all waits for every replica currently in the ISR; with all three in sync that is three, and min.insync.replicas=2 keeps a write from being acknowledged on fewer than two.

must_not.text: Sides with the rule and recommends keeping min.insync.replicas=3 on ledger-entries (accepting the errors on every patch run).
must_not.consequence: The writer keeps failing for minutes on every broker restart, with no gain in durability over replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 that the team could actually use.
must_not.condition: Counts if keeping 3 is the recommendation. Raising the replication factor would be a correct alternative only with disk room, which the question rules out.
must_not.near_miss: With replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2 is the documented durable setting; 3 leaves no room for a single restart.

reference:
The team is right; lowering to 2 is the correct change here, done at the right moment.

With replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 3, every one of the three replicas must be in the ISR for an acks=all write to succeed. Any broker restart takes a replica out of the ISR of every partition it hosts, so writes fail until it is back: that is what each patch run shows. Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 is the documented durable setup: every acknowledged write is still on at least two replicas, and one broker can be down. The rule 'never lower it' is meant to stop people going to 1, which would allow single-copy acknowledgements; do not do that, and keep acks=all.

How:
1. Check replication factor 3 on all 12 partitions (kafka-topics.sh --describe) and that the ISR is complete everywhere, as it is today.
2. Do it outside the patch run: with ELR enabled (default since the cluster was created on 4.2), changing a topic's min.insync.replicas clears its ELR state.
3. Either drop the override to fall back to the cluster default:
   bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name ledger-entries --delete-config min.insync.replicas
   or set it explicitly with --add-config min.insync.replicas=2.
4. Verify with --describe, and in the next patch run watch UnderMinIsrPartitionCount stay 0 and the writer stay free of NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Lower it, to 2, not 1. A min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor means acks=all succeeds only when all three replicas are in sync, so the routine restart of any one broker blocks writes to its partitions; 3 buys no tolerance at all. RF 3 with min ISR 2 is the configuration the Kafka docs give as the typical durable one: an acknowledged write has at least two copies and a single broker can be offline. First confirm all partitions have three replicas and a full ISR. Then remove the topic override (kafka-configs.sh --entity-type topics --entity-name ledger-entries --alter --delete-config min.insync.replicas) so the cluster default of 2 applies, or add-config the value 2. Pick a calm moment rather than the middle of a roll, because a topic-level min.insync.replicas change resets that topic's eligible leader replicas. Check the next patch night for NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS.
generic: min.insync.replicas controls how many replicas must acknowledge a write with acks=all. Higher values improve durability but reduce availability. Choose a value that matches your requirements, typically less than the replication factor, and test the behaviour during broker restarts.
note: destructive_right: lowering a safeguard is the correct action, under the check in m1 and m3. The generic answer says 'typically less than the replication factor' without recommending a change; it makes no must point. Nearest earlier item p2-21 is about the cluster-level value created from the controllers with ELR; here the family is a topic override equal to the replication factor that blocks every roll, and the ELR fact is the timing condition. The describe output's ELR columns are empty because no partition is below min ISR. Second review: n2 replaced (the ELR timing harm did not hold, see the changes file); m3 kept as a weight-1 order point without the implied risk; n3 (keep 3) stays wrong: the cost of refusing is the recurring write failures the team already has, not new damage.
